findings.headline: General Fund services overspent by £799k, only achieving balance through one-off grants and interest income
findings.detail: The Cost of Services (General Fund) overran budget by £799,306. After accounting for Sport and Leisure trading profits, the council faced a £670k shortfall. This was covered only through additional interest income (£578,787) and a National Insurance grant (£141,785), leaving a narrow £50k surplus.
findings.matters: The council's operational services ran approximately 9% over budget. The final surplus depends on interest income and discretionary grants, not on operational control. This suggests structural cost pressures or budget management challenges.
findings.figures: Cost of Services overspend £799,306; additional interest income £578,787; National Insurance grant £141,785; final surplus £50,460
findings.quote: This is offset by grant and additional interest income giving a final surplus position of £50k.

findings.headline: £468k overspend in Property Services due to business rates on empty commercial properties and lost rental income
findings.detail: The Resources directorate overspent by £387k overall, with Property Services showing an overspend of £468,247. This is driven by costs of maintaining empty commercial properties and the resulting loss of rental income that would normally offset those costs.
findings.matters: Empty commercial property holdings represent dead weight on council finances and suggest either portfolio management issues or a struggling commercial real estate market in the borough. Lost rental income reduces the council's revenue base.
findings.figures: £468,247 overspend in Property Services
findings.quote: This is mainly due to the cost of business rates for empty commercial properties and the associated loss of rental income.

findings.headline: Housing benefit subsidy shortfall of £642k due to temporary accommodation costs exceeding central government reimbursement
findings.detail: The Planning and Place directorate overspent by £534k, with the Benefits and Council Tax service showing an overspend of £641,858. The council states that spending on temporary accommodation for homeless people exceeds the amount it can reclaim through the benefit subsidy system.
findings.matters: This reveals structural demand pressure in temporary accommodation that the council cannot fully recoup. As homelessness continues to rise, this gap is likely to recur and widen.
findings.figures: £641,858 overspend in Benefits and Council Tax service
findings.quote: This shortfall is caused by a difference in the rental costs of short-term accommodation and the amount that can be reclaimed through the benefit subsidy system.

findings.headline: Hope Nursery self-build plots and Burford Street car park developments remain on hold with no progress.
findings.detail: Two capital projects, Hope Nursery (£863k) and Burford Street car park (£53k), have neither budget spend nor explanation of why they are on hold or when they might proceed.
findings.matters: Projects on hold represent delayed service delivery and capital that has been budgeted but cannot be deployed, affecting the council's capital expenditure efficiency.
findings.figures: Hope Nursery budget £863,000, £0 spent; Burford Street budget £53,000, £0 spent
findings.quote: Hope Nursery – Self build plots 863 0 (863) On hold

findings.headline: Theobalds Business Park Phase 2 is reconsidering its development model with options for a joint development being considered.
findings.detail: This £1m project has only 27% spend to date (£266k) and the monitor states that options for joint development are being considered, suggesting a potential change in approach. No detail is given on timing or what this means for the project.
findings.matters: A change in development model for a major project could delay completion, change funding requirements, or affect the council's financial returns from the site.
findings.figures: Budget £1,000,000; Actual and committed spend £266,934 (27%); Estimated completion 2027/28
findings.quote: Options for a joint development are being considered.

findings.headline: A10 Major Road Network scheme remains paused awaiting Department for Transport response to business case submitted in October 2023.
findings.detail: The council has £3.1m allocated to A10 improvements and has spent only £764k (25%). In March 2026 the government confirmed the scheme remains in the Major Road Network Programme, but the council is still awaiting a formal response on the Strategic Outline Business Case submitted nearly 18 months ago. This response will determine whether the project can progress to the next stage.
findings.matters: A major infrastructure project affecting the local area cannot proceed without government approval, creating uncertainty about capital spending and service delivery for the area the council serves.
findings.figures: Budget £3,091,000; Actual and committed spend £764,224 (25%); Strategic Outline Business Case submitted October 2023
findings.quote: In March 2026 the government confirmed that the A10 Improvement Scheme at Broxbourne will remain part of the Major Road Network Programme. This confirmation is expected to trigger a formal response from the Department for Transport regarding the Strategic Outline Business Case submitted in October 2023.

findings.headline: Bishops College New River Development has spent only £2k of £1.5m budget with completion still targeted for 2026/27.
findings.detail: This project has virtually no spend to date (£2k out of £1.5m) yet is still estimated to complete in 2026/27. There is no narrative explanation in the monitor of what is happening with this development.
findings.matters: A £1.5m project with near-zero progress cannot realistically complete within the year, creating a delivery risk and raising questions about project management and realistic forecasting.
findings.figures: Budget £1,500,000; Actual and committed spend £2,000; Estimated completion 2026/27
findings.quote: Bishops College New River Development  1,500 2 (1,498) 2026/27

findings.headline: John Warner Sports Centre £4.5m facilities upgrade has spent only 1.5% by end of Q4 with tender not published until late June 2026, risking the 2026/27 completion target.
findings.detail: The sports centre upgrade is allocated £4.5m but has only £68k actual and committed spend at end of March 2026. Design work is underway and architects have been appointed, but the tender is not expected until late June/early July 2026. With completion targeted for 2026/27, this timeline is extremely tight.
findings.matters: A £4.5m capital project for a major leisure facility with so little progress and so little time before handover creates delivery risk, potential cost overruns, and service disruption.
findings.figures: Budget £4,500,000; Actual and committed spend £68,350 (1.5%); Estimated completion 2026/27
findings.quote: Work is being carried out on the design element of the refurbishment. Architects have been appointed. The tender is expected to be published late June early July 2026.

findings.headline: Two servers running on unsupported operating system more than 13 months after vendor support ended
findings.detail: Two servers were identified running an operating system that expired in May 2025. At the time of this audit in June 2026, this represents over a year of operation on unsupported software with no security updates. This creates both security and compliance exposure.
findings.matters: Running on expired/unsupported operating systems increases vulnerability to security exploits and violates standard IT compliance practices, potentially affecting systems that handle council financial data.
findings.figures: 2 servers; OS expired May 2025
findings.quote: The review highlighted that two additional servers were running on an operating system which had expired in May 2025.

findings.headline: Internal Audit function operating at reduced capacity due to multiple long-term sickness absences
findings.detail: The audit team is currently under significant staffing pressure with multiple concurrent long-term sicknesses. Management has implemented a revised delivery plan with audits re-prioritised by risk, though the S151 Officer is closely monitoring the situation.
findings.matters: Internal Audit is a core control function; staffing shortages reduce the council's ability to assure that financial and operational controls are effective, creating gaps in governance oversight.
findings.figures: multiple long-term sickness absences
findings.quote: The service has been operating with reduced capacity this quarter as a result of multiple long-term sickness absences within the team. While this has created pressure on delivery, the situation is being managed proactively.

findings.headline: Overdue audit recommendations have increased 50% in one year, with medium-priority items more than doubling
findings.detail: The number of overdue recommendations grew from 6 in May 2025 to 9 in May 2026. Medium-priority overdue recommendations more than doubled from 4 to 8 during the same period. The council has recently introduced six-weekly tracking to address implementation delays.
findings.matters: A growing backlog of overdue audit recommendations indicates the council is not implementing identified control improvements promptly, leaving known risks unaddressed and weakening the control environment.
findings.figures: May 2025: 6 overdue (4 medium, 1 low); May 2026: 9 overdue (8 medium, 1 low)
findings.quote: The current tracker (Appendix H) contains nine overdue recommendations; a comparison with three previous periods is given in the table below.

findings.headline: Land and buildings revaluation model creates risk of material misstatement
findings.detail: The council has adopted a rolling revaluation model where land and buildings are revalued over a five-year cycle with indexation applied in intervening years. The auditor identifies risk that assets not revalued in a given year may differ materially from fair value if the indexation applied is not appropriate.
findings.matters: Land and buildings are major assets on the balance sheet. Improper valuation through inappropriate indexation could materially misstate net worth and the council's asset base.
findings.figures: Five-year revaluation cycle with indexation in intervening years
findings.quote: The Authority has adopted a rolling revaluation model which sees all land and buildings revalued over a five-year cycle and indexation in the intervening years. This creates a risk that the carrying value of assets not revalued in year differs materially from the year end current value as the indexation applied is not appropriate.

findings.headline: Investment property portfolio of £126m carries significant valuation risk
findings.detail: As at 31 March 2025, the council held investment properties valued at £126m. The auditor identifies significant risk that these properties are not held at fair value as required by the accounting code. Significant judgement is required to assess fair value, and valuations must reflect market conditions at each reporting period.
findings.matters: £126m represents a material balance (approximately 58 times the audit materiality threshold of £2.1m). Valuation errors could significantly affect the council's net asset position and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £126m investment property valuation as at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: As of 31 March 2025, the Council had investment properties with total value of £126 m. There is a risk that investment properties are not being held at fair value, as is required by the Code. Significant judgement is required to assess fair value and management experts are often engaged to undertake the valuations.

findings.headline: Audit opinions have been disclaimed for two consecutive years (2023/24 and 2024/25)
findings.detail: The council received a disclaimed audit opinion for 2023/24 (issued 28 February 2025) and a further disclaimed opinion for 2024/25 (issued 27 February 2026). This means there is no external audit assurance over the financial statements for these two years. The auditor is now in the process of rebuilding assurance for 2025/26.
findings.matters: Lenders cannot rely on verified financial statements for two complete years. This is a material weakness in financial reporting assurance and increases uncertainty about the council's true financial position.
findings.figures: 2023/24 and 2024/25 financial years
findings.quote: We then issued a disclaimer of opinion for 2023/24 on 28 February 2025 to comply with the statutory backstop date as reported to you previously. For the 2024/25 audit we issued a disclaimed opinion on 27 February 2026.

findings.paper_title: App A BoB Internal Audit 2025_26 summary
findings.headline: Cemetery income shortfall in 2024/25 remains unexplained despite investigation
findings.detail: Internal audit investigated the cause of a shortfall in cemetery income during 2024/25 but could not identify the root cause, raising questions about the strength of income controls and reconciliation in this area.
findings.matters: Unexplained income losses indicate either control weaknesses or undetected losses through error or fraud
findings.figures: shortfall in income for cemeteries in 2024/25
findings.quote: IA explored the reasons for a shortfall in income for cemeteries in 2024/25. The cause of the shortfall could not be identified but recommendations were agreed to strengthen the reconciliation process and adding more detail when updating systems.

findings.paper_title: App A BoB Internal Audit 2025_26 summary
findings.headline: Temporary workers spending lacks central monitoring and manager guidance
findings.detail: An audit of temporary workers spending found control weaknesses: no central system monitors the spend, and managers have no detailed guidance on procedures to follow.
findings.matters: Absence of central monitoring creates risk of uncontrolled temporary staffing spend and inability to detect overspending or policy breaches
findings.figures: no central monitoring and no detailed guidance
findings.quote: Weaknesses were found in that there was no central monitoring and no detailed guidance for managers.

findings.paper_title: App A BoB Internal Audit 2025_26 summary
findings.headline: Multiple IT security vulnerabilities persist including unsupported systems, delayed patching, outdated devices, and unupdated antivirus signatures
findings.detail: The IT change and patch management audit identified that whilst processes are well-defined, several active security vulnerabilities remain due to systems still in use past end-of-support, patches delayed, devices not current, and antivirus protections not kept up to date.
findings.matters: Unresolved security vulnerabilities in core systems create material risk of data breach, ransomware infection, or unplanned service failure
findings.figures: several security vulnerabilities remain
findings.quote: ICT change management processes are well-defined and functioning, but several security vulnerabilities remain due to unsupported systems, delayed patching, outdated devices, and antivirus signatures not being kept up to date.

findings.paper_title: App A BoB Internal Audit 2025_26 summary
findings.headline: IT disaster recovery has three outstanding recommendations from the prior audit despite claims of full implementation
findings.detail: The council claimed all recommendations from the 2022 IT DR audit had been fully implemented following transition to a new IT service provider. However, fieldwork revealed this assurance was not substantiated: three recommendations remain outstanding, with an action plan now in place.
findings.matters: Unresolved IT disaster recovery weaknesses create risk of unplanned service interruption and inability to restore operations after an incident
findings.figures: three recommendations remain outstanding
findings.quote: Limited assurance was given at the previous audit in November 2022; since then the Council has transitioned to a new IT service provider. Internal Audit was assured that all recommendations from the prior audit had been fully implemented. However, this assurance has not been substantiated, as three recommendations remain outstanding.

findings.paper_title: App B 2025-26 Audit Plan Year End position
findings.headline: IT Disaster Recovery received Limited assurance from internal audit
findings.detail: The council's IT disaster recovery controls audit concluded with Limited assurance and identified 1 high recommendation and 4 medium recommendations. Limited is the lowest assurance opinion the audit provides.
findings.matters: Limited assurance in disaster recovery indicates significant deficiencies in the council's ability to recover critical financial systems, which threatens business continuity and the integrity of financial data and controls
findings.figures: 1 high recommendation, 4 medium recommendations
findings.quote: IT Disaster Recovery (DR) Finance 12 Final report Limited 1 4 0

findings.headline: External auditors issued a disclaimed opinion on 2024/25 accounts due to audit completion delays
findings.detail: KPMG could not complete their audit of the 2024/25 financial statements by the required 27 February 2026 deadline and issued a disclaimed opinion. The council notes this was common across most councils and emphasises that a disclaimer does not indicate material misstatement, only that auditors could not obtain sufficient evidence in time.
findings.matters: A lender depends on independently audited financial statements. A disclaimed opinion reduces assurance about account accuracy even though the council reports no suspected errors.
findings.figures: 27 February 2026 deadline
findings.quote: because auditors could not finish their work by that date, they were required to issue a disclaimed opinion. A disclaimer means the auditor could not obtain sufficient evidence in time, not that the accounts were materially misstated.

findings.headline: Council is pursuing three major capital investment schemes totalling over £400m in partnership with HCC and government funding
findings.detail: The council is working with Hertfordshire County Council on a £400m mixed-use development at Brookfield Riverside plus an adjacent Brookfield Garden Village. The council is also deploying £14.3m in Levelling Up Funds for Waltham Cross town centre regeneration and hosting a new Google data centre adjacent to the council-owned Theobalds Enterprise Centre.
findings.matters: These major capital commitments represent significant financial exposure and will require sustained governance and delivery through the LGR transition period. A lender needs visibility of major capital schemes and their financing.
findings.figures: £400m Brookfield Riverside scheme; £14.3m Levelling Up Funds for Waltham Cross; Google data centre (amount not specified)
findings.quote: Notable examples include working with Hertfordshire County Council (HCC) to deliver the £400M mixed use scheme at Brookfield Riverside and the adjacent Brookfield Garden Village. Recently using the £14.3M of Levelling Up Funds for the regeneration of Waltham Cross town centre and the building of a new data centre by Google adjacent to the Council owned Theobalds Enterprise Centre.

findings.headline: External auditors gave a disclaimed opinion on 2024-25 accounts due to insufficient audit evidence within backstop timeframes
findings.detail: KPMG was unable to obtain sufficient audit evidence within the timeframes imposed under backstop arrangements to give a full audit opinion on the 2024-25 Statement of Accounts. While the council notes this is not unique to Broxbourne and affects other councils, there is a plan in place over the next few years to build assurances and resolve this issue.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion means the auditor could not fully verify the financial statements, creating uncertainty about financial reporting quality and control effectiveness.
findings.figures: 2024-25 accounts; plan to build assurances over coming years
findings.quote: As in recent years external audit gave a disclaimed audit opinion on the basis that they were unable to obtain sufficient audit evidence due to the timeframes imposed under backstop arrangements (and is not unique to Broxbourne). There is a plan in place with KPMG on how assurances can be built over the next few years.

findings.headline: Multiple services report single points of failure and gaps in succession planning
findings.detail: The council has identified team resilience as an ongoing governance risk, particularly in small teams and specialist roles. Services report limited capacity to provide emergency cover and succession planning gaps. While managers have implemented local mitigations such as cross-training and external support, these control weaknesses are particularly concerning during the LGR transition period.
findings.matters: Single points of failure in key teams create operational risk and could affect the council's ability to execute financial management, audit responses, and regulatory compliance.
findings.figures: No specific numbers quantified
findings.quote: Several services report single points of failure, limited capacity to provide cover, and gaps in succession planning. While managers have put local mitigations in place, such as cross-training, handover notes and use of external support, these issues present an ongoing governance risk, especially during the transition to the new authority.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates significant strategic uncertainty with vesting day set for April 2028
findings.detail: All 11 Hertfordshire councils submitted a joint proposal to government on 28 November 2025 for Local Government Reorganisation. The final government decision was expected summer 2026 (at the time of this statement). The council is now in transition planning, requiring additional resources and strengthened governance arrangements. This represents a major organizational change that will affect service delivery and financial management over the next two years.
findings.matters: Organizational restructuring on this scale creates material delivery, financial and control risks during a critical borrowing period. The council must maintain service continuity while managing a major transition.
findings.figures: Vesting day 1 April 2028; 11 councils submitted joint proposal 28 November 2025
findings.quote: LGR represents a significant strategic uncertainty for Broxbourne, requiring additional resources, careful risk management, and strengthened governance arrangements to maintain service delivery and organisational stability.

findings.headline: Prior year audit opinions were disclaimed, requiring additional audit work and unpriced costs in the current year.
findings.detail: The council received disclaimed audit opinions in the prior year (meaning the auditor could not fully validate the financial statements). KPMG will undertake additional work to address these issues, but has not included the cost of this remediation in the planned audit fee. The specific prior year issues and current year significance are detailed in a separate audit planning report.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion signals the auditor could not complete or validate the prior year financial statements, raising questions about the council's financial controls and reporting that would concern lenders assessing financial stability.
findings.figures: Audit fee £173,465 for 2025/26 (prior year £168,741), excluding additional costs for prior year remediation work.
findings.quote: any additional work required as a result of the disclaimed prior year opinions

findings.headline: Brookfield development consuming £3.5m in 2026/27 and £12m in 2027/28
findings.detail: The capital programme allocates £3.5m for 'implementation of the sale and construction of Brookfield Riverside and Brookfield Garden Village' in 2026/27, rising to £12m in 2027/28. This represents 92% of one-off projects and 75% of total capital spend, funded from the Brookfield reserve.
findings.matters: A £15.5m development commitment over two years is material for a council of this size; lenders would want to understand project status, delivery risk, and whether the Brookfield reserve is adequately sized.
findings.quote: Brookfield 3,500,000 12,000,000 Brookfield reserve Implementation of the sale and construction of Brookfield Riverside and Brookfield Garden Village.

findings.headline: Council authorises up to £1 million drawdown from reserves for Local Government Reorganisation costs
findings.detail: The resolution authorises the Chief Executive to drawdown up to £1 million from reserves specifically to fund Local Government Reorganisation costs. This indicates the council is preparing for anticipated structural changes and will use reserves rather than revenue funding to cover these costs.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdowns for reorganisation signal anticipated institutional restructuring, and using reserves for this purpose means those funds are not available as a buffer against other financial pressures.
findings.figures: £1 million from reserves
findings.quote: To authorise the Chief Executive to approve the drawdown of up to £1million from reserves to fund Local Government Reorganisation costs.

findings.headline: Council holds capital investment in wholly-owned subsidiary (Badger BC Investments Ltd) with declining loan repayment stream
findings.detail: Council made a £1.403m capital investment in Badger BC Investments Ltd in 2024/25. Loan repayments from the subsidiary contribute to capital receipts: £1.591m (2024/25) declining to £203k (2026/27) and £225k (2027/28).
findings.matters: Lenders would need visibility on subsidiary performance and the reasons for declining repayment stream; the absence of disclosure on subsidiary assets and operations creates uncertainty about this exposure
findings.quote: Repayments of loans made to other organisations (such as its wholly-owned subsidiary Badger BC Investments Ltd) also generate capital receipts.

findings.headline: Capital strategy explicitly centred on enhancing income-generating property assets to fund revenue resilience
findings.detail: Council's capital priorities focus on expanding and maintaining property assets to generate revenue income, rather than traditional service-provision capital. This reflects a strategy to offset grant reductions and maintain financial sustainability through asset income.
findings.matters: Revenue sustainability becomes dependent on property valuations and rental income streams; any decline in asset values or rental income would directly impact debt serviceability and financial position
findings.figures: No specific asset portfolio figures disclosed; capital programme explicitly focused on income-generating assets
findings.quote: the focus within the capital programme is on enhancing the Council's existing income generating assets to safeguard long-term revenue income streams.

findings.headline: Council forecasts net interest income from treasury and subsidiary operations despite £51.65m outstanding borrowing
findings.detail: Table 7 shows financing costs of (£701)k forecast for 2026/27, indicating net income rather than net cost. This results because interest income from treasury investments and subsidiary loans exceeds borrowing costs.
findings.matters: Lenders would need to assess sustainability of this income — whether it derives from high treasury returns (cyclical risk in a rising-rate environment) or subsidiary asset performance (underlying concentration risk)
findings.figures: Financing costs: (£886)k actual 2024/25 → (£701)k estimated 2026/27; borrowing outstanding: £51.650m; capital financing requirement: £57.130m
findings.quote: The Council's interest payable on borrowing for 2026/27 is forecast lower than the interest income it receives on treasury management investments and from the loans it makes.

findings.headline: Capital programme forecast to grow while dependent on shrinking external funding and modest capital receipts
findings.detail: Capital expenditure estimated to rise from £15.333m (2026/27) to £17.763m (2027/28), while external sources remain minimal (£1.054m to £2.371m) and capital receipts are low (£0.517m to £0.539m). Own resources must continue to fund the shortfall.
findings.matters: Growing capital ambitions financed primarily from reserves creates sustainability risk if reserves are not sufficient or capital receipt streams decline further
findings.quote: In 2026/27, the Council has planned capital expenditure of £15.3 million as summarised below, this includes an estimated £10.6 million carried forward from the current year

findings.headline: External capital funding collapses; council shifts to financing capital from own resources
findings.detail: External sources (grants, s106 contributions) decline from £11.51m forecast in 2025/26 to £1.054m in 2026/27 — a 91% drop. Own resources must fund £14.279m of a £15.333m capital programme (93%), up sharply from prior years.
findings.matters: Reliance on own resources and capital receipts to finance capital expenditure raises questions about reserve depletion and financial flexibility if external funding sources do not recover
findings.figures: External sources: £11.51m (2025/26) → £1.054m (2026/27); own resources: £14.279m (2026/27); total capital: £15.333m
findings.quote: All capital expenditure must be financed either from external sources (such as s106 contributions), the Council's own resources (revenue contribution to capital, reserves and capital receipts) or prudential borrowing.

findings.paper_title: GENERAL FUND BUDGETS INCLUDING FEES AND CHARGES 202627_v2
findings.headline: Broxbourne Sport and Spotlight leisure trading deficits growing to £555k, up from £477k in 2025/26
findings.detail: The two leisure trading arms show combined deficits of £555k in 2026/27, an increase of £78k year-on-year. Despite continued membership growth and revenue improvements, the deficits are growing due to inflationary pressures, particularly the 4.1% National Living Wage increase. These deficits are funded from business rates income.
findings.matters: Shows growing annual subsidy requirement for leisure services despite operational improvements, indicating structural cost inflation outpacing revenue growth
findings.figures: Broxbourne Sport £148k, Spotlight £407k, combined £555k versus £477k in 2025/26
findings.quote: The projected combined deficit for Broxbourne Sport (£148k) and the Spotlight (£407k) for 2026/27 is £555k; this is compared to a budgeted deficit in 2025/26 of £477k.

findings.paper_title: GENERAL FUND BUDGETS INCLUDING FEES AND CHARGES 202627_v2
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates unquantified costs and potential council abolition in 2028
findings.detail: Hertfordshire submitted a joint LGR proposal in November 2025 proposing creation of new unitary councils. Broxbourne is told the current authority is expected to be abolished in 2028 if reorganisation proceeds. The council is setting aside up to £1m for transition costs but states the actual value is not yet quantified and may include indirect costs such as backfilling officer roles seconded to the programme.
findings.matters: Creates medium-term existential uncertainty affecting strategic and financial planning, with unquantified costs requiring up to £1m reserve drawdown and potential impact on service continuity
findings.figures: Up to £1 million from Service Protection and Enhancement Reserve (projected £3.8m balance at 31 March 2026)
findings.quote: the current authority is expected to be abolished in 2028 if Government proceeds with reorganisation... the value of this contribution has not yet been quantified

findings.paper_title: GENERAL FUND BUDGETS INCLUDING FEES AND CHARGES 202627_v2
findings.headline: Broxbourne Environmental Services Trading Ltd contract uplift of £1.2 million to address historical pricing underperformance
findings.detail: The council's wholly-owned subsidiary contract was renewed in 2026 after expiry in March 2026. During renewal, the council recognised that previous contract price increases had not kept pace with inflation, creating a financial imbalance. To address this, a £1.2m uplift to contract pricing was agreed, representing a material increase to maintain service continuity.
findings.matters: Shows a critical outsourced service requiring retroactive cost recovery due to previous pricing not keeping pace with inflation, indicating potential contract management issues and ongoing cost pressures
findings.figures: £1.2 million contract price adjustment uplift
findings.quote: It was recognised during the review process that previous contract price increases had not kept pace with inflation, resulting in a financial imbalance. To address this, the Council has agreed to an uplift in the contract price adjustment of £1.2 million.

findings.headline: Investment income budget is vulnerable to falling interest rates in 2026/27
findings.detail: Council budgets for £2.31m investment income at 3.84% for 2026/27, but has been advised that 'investment yields will fall during the interest rate cutting cycle.' With Bank of England rate cuts expected, actual returns will likely underperform the budget assumption.
findings.matters: Debt service cost (£2.3m) is nearly equal to budgeted investment income (£2.31m); any shortfall creates budget pressure. Council has explicitly flagged this risk.
findings.figures: Investment income budget £2,310,000 at 3.84%; debt interest budget £2,299,617 on £51.65m average debt
findings.quote: The Council has been advised that investment yields will fall during the interest rate cutting cycle in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Council is drawing down cash reserves instead of borrowing; reserves will shrink further as capital programme runs
findings.detail: Council holds £53m in investments but only £51.65m in debt. This under-borrowed position is intentional: cash reserves are being used to cover what would normally be borrowed, betting rates will fall. As the capital programme delivers, these investments will 'continue to reduce,' further depleting reserves.
findings.matters: Reduces the council's financial cushion; if capital programme accelerates, unexpected costs arise, or rate forecasts miss, council loses flexibility to borrow on its terms
findings.figures: £53m investments as of December 2025, forecast to fall to approximately £51m by 31 March 2027
findings.quote: Capital expenditure and the availability of the Council's own resources (usable reserves) will dictate the Council's borrowing requirement.

findings.headline: £51.65m of short-term debt matures April-September 2026 and must be refinanced
findings.detail: All of the council's borrowing consists of short-term loans from other local authorities, all maturing in the next six months. The council plans to refinance via the short-term market, betting that short-dated rates will remain lower than longer-term alternatives.
findings.matters: Significant refinancing event requiring execution; council depends on counterparties continuing to lend and on rates falling as forecast
findings.figures: £51.65m at rates 4.15%-4.65%, all maturing April-September 2026
findings.quote: These loans mature between April and September 2026 and will need to be refinanced.

findings.headline: £15.5m in outstanding loans to wholly-owned subsidiary Badger BC Investments Ltd with no upper limit restriction.
findings.detail: The council makes loans to wholly-owned subsidiaries with no restriction on the value. As at 31 March 2025, Badger BC Investments Ltd held assets valued at £18.9m against outstanding loans of £15.5m. These loans are made at 4.50% interest. The council retains full control to compel repayment by forcing asset sales if required.
findings.matters: Unlimited lending to a subsidiary concentrates financial risk in a single entity; while assets currently cover loans, the absence of a maximum exposure limit creates potential risk if the subsidiary underperforms or asset values decline.
findings.figures: Badger BC Investments Ltd: assets £18.9m; outstanding loans £15.5m; loan interest rate 4.50%
findings.quote: There will be no restriction on the value of loans to the wholly owned subsidiary companies.

findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio yield declining from 7.1% to 6.9%, moving closer to the council's 6% minimum threshold.
findings.detail: Portfolio yield fell from 7.1% actual in 2024/25 to forecast 6.7% in 2025/26 and estimated 6.9% in 2026/27. The council has set a minimum yield expectation of 6%, stating it will only invest below this level if the investment fulfils other strategic interests. The declining trend suggests either portfolio composition is changing or market conditions are affecting returns.
findings.matters: Declining yields reduce income available to support services; if the decline continues, the council may struggle to maintain current service funding from property investment returns.
findings.figures: 2024/25 actual: 7.1%; 2025/26 forecast: 6.7%; 2026/27 estimate: 6.9%; minimum yield threshold: 6%
findings.quote: The Council has a minimum yield expectation of 6% and will only invest in a property below this level if it fulfils other strategic interests.

findings.headline: Council budgets for 28% of net service expenditure to come from commercial property rental income, explicitly instead of cutting services.
findings.detail: The council states it invests in commercial properties 'in preference to reducing or cutting services, which would be necessary in order to set a balanced budget when expenditure is increasing due to inflationary pressures and changes in demand for services and government funding is reducing.' Commercial rental income is budgeted at £9,030k in 2026/27 against net service expenditure of £31,686k. A rental income protection reserve (£2.164m as at 31 March 2025) is maintained to cover short-term shortfalls.
findings.matters: A lender would need to understand that the council's financial resilience depends significantly on continued commercial rental income; any deterioration in that income stream would require service cuts or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: 2026/27: commercial rent income £9,030k against net service expenditure of £31,686k (28%); rental income protection reserve £2.164m as at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: It chooses to do this in preference to reducing or cutting services, which would be necessary in order to set a balanced budget when expenditure is increasing due to inflationary pressures and changes in demand for services and government funding is reducing.

findings.headline: £927k year-end funding gap with decision on reserve drawdown deferred until end of financial year
findings.detail: The General Fund projects a total overspend of £1,705k. After accounting for additional interest income (£421k) and grant income (£129k), a remaining gap of £927k is unresolved. The council explicitly states that 'the decision on how to fund the remaining balance of £927k will be made towards the end of the financial year when the amount and causes have been crystallised.' Potential funding sources identified are the Service Specific Grant Reserve (£1.3m held for temporary accommodation investment) or the Rental Income Protection Reserve (£2,163k).
findings.matters: Shows the council cannot balance its operations within-year from income sources and must resort to reserve drawdown. The deferred decision to year-end suggests insufficient certainty about the causes of overspend at mid-year. Drawing on the Service Specific Grant Reserve would reduce funds available for planned temporary accommodation investment.
findings.figures: £1,705k total General Fund overspend; £421k additional interest income; £129k grant income; £927k unresolved funding gap; Service Specific Grant Reserve £1.3m; Rental Income Protection Reserve £2,163k
findings.quote: The decision on how to fund the remaining balance of £927k will be made towards the end of the financial year when the amount and causes have been crystallised.

findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio generating £359k operational overspend from voids, business rates on empty units, and lost rental income
findings.detail: Property Services forecasts an overspend of £359k in the Resources directorate due to empty commercial properties. The council is incurring business rates and insurance costs on multiple void units with no rental income. Specific properties in void include 5 Burnt Oak, Edgeware (new lease being negotiated at £125k p.a., creating a £145.7k annual shortfall from budget), multiple Turnford Place units, and 49 Hoddesdon Industrial Centre. The council has appointed a new lettings agent at Turnford Place in attempt to remarket units, but expects rent-free periods will be offered to attract tenants.
findings.matters: Shows ongoing property portfolio management challenges. The council is carrying assets at a loss while attempting to remarket them. The Rental Income Protection Reserve (£2,163k current balance) is being drawn to absorb these recurring losses rather than being available for operational use.
findings.figures: £359k Property Services overspend; 5 Burnt Oak rent shortfall £145.7k; Turnford Place combined budgeted rent £451.6k; Rental Income Protection Reserve balance £2,163k
findings.quote: This is due to the cost of business rates for empty commercial properties, reduced rental income and higher than budgeted insurance costs due to empty properties.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation portfolio contains 44 pre-booked properties with significant voids due to lower-than-forecast single-person unit demand
findings.detail: The Housing and Homelessness service forecasts an overspend of £138.5k. The council maintains approximately 44 nightly-booked temporary accommodation properties to ensure supply, but demand for single-person units has been lower than budgeted, leaving many properties void. These empty units incur running costs and maintenance with no offsetting rental income. In response, the council is closing the Cromwell Avenue site, which predominantly comprises single-person units, to reduce further costs.
findings.matters: Shows demand forecasting error and poor portfolio management. The council has overcommitted to single-person accommodation supply and is carrying properties at a loss. Forced closure creates future supply risk if demand for this unit type resurfaces.
findings.figures: £138.5k overspend in Housing and Homelessness; approximately 44 properties pre-booked; void units generating zero rental income; Cromwell Avenue site closure to reduce costs
findings.quote: There are approximately 44 nightly paid properties pre-booked on a rolling basis to ensure temporary accommodation is readily available. However, there has been less demand for single person units, meaning that many of these units are void. Therefore, no rental income has been received to offset the cost.

findings.headline: Housing benefit subsidy income projected to shortfall by £1,278k as temporary accommodation costs exceed what the benefit system reimburses
findings.detail: The Benefits and Council Tax service faces an overspend of £1,278k on housing benefit subsidy income specifically. This arises because the cost of providing temporary accommodation exceeds the amount the council can reclaim through the benefit subsidy system. The shortfall is driven by both increased demand for temporary accommodation and the higher costs associated with providing it. This is identified as the main risk area in the monitor.
findings.matters: Shows structural mismatch between service obligations and available funding. The council has been asked to house more homeless people, but the benefit system does not reimburse the full cost of doing so. This places ongoing structural pressure on the budget and is unlikely to resolve without intervention.
findings.figures: £1,278k overspend on housing benefit subsidy; Benefits and Council Tax budget £1,998,099 vs projected outturn £3,276,488
findings.quote: This is due to an increase in both demand and the costs of providing temporary accommodation that cannot be fully recovered by housing benefit subsidy.

findings.headline: Waltham Cross High Street car park resurfacing locked until public realm works complete
findings.detail: The £175k resurfacing project cannot progress because the area is being used as a site compound for the Waltham Cross Town Centre regeneration works. This dependency means the project remains entirely underspent and cannot start until the primary works are complete.
findings.matters: Project sequencing dependencies lock up capital budgets and prevent deployment, potentially creating year-end budget pressure or carry-forward if the primary regeneration works experience delay.
findings.figures: £175,000 budget; £0 spent; £175,000 underspend
findings.quote: This work cannot be progressed until the Waltham Cross public realm works are complete as the area is being used as a site compound.

findings.headline: Grundy Park improvements: contractor claim for delay and disruption under council dispute
findings.detail: Main works at Grundy Park were completed within budget (£1.35m spent of £1.45m budget), but the contractor has submitted a claim citing delay and disruption which the council is disputing. Other potential works including remediation of the listed boundary wall are pending resolution of this claim.
findings.matters: An unresolved contractor dispute could result in additional unanticipated costs and extended litigation, creating financial uncertainty beyond the current project and delaying follow-up works.
findings.figures: £1,447,650 total budget; £1,349,135 spent; £98,515 underspend
findings.quote: There is a claim from the contractor citing delay and disruption which the Council is disputing. Other potential works in and around the park, including remediation of the listed boundary wall, are pending resolution of the claim.

findings.headline: Major Road Network A10 upgrade awaiting Department for Transport strategic outline business case approval
findings.detail: The council is working with Hertfordshire County Council to prepare a business case for Department for Transport funding for major A10 upgrades. The Department is currently reviewing the strategic outline business case. Only £684k has been spent of the £3.1m budgeted amount.
findings.matters: A significant infrastructure project depends on external government approval; failure to progress past the strategic phase could force the council to reprioritise or reduce this capital commitment.
findings.figures: £3,091,383 budget; £684,266 spent; £2,407,117 underspend
findings.quote: The Department for Transport is reviewing the strategic outline business case and the Council is awaiting a response.

findings.headline: John Warner Sports Centre £4.5m facilities upgrade has not commenced pending lease agreement
findings.detail: A design partner has been appointed for the £4.5m facilities upgrade, but works cannot commence until the lease agreement is signed. As at end Q2, no expenditure has been recorded against this major project, representing a 100% underspend.
findings.matters: A major capital project is stalled pending lease negotiation; delay could affect service delivery and community provision, and extend the capital spending profile if negotiation extends beyond the financial year.
findings.figures: £4,500,000 budget; £0 spent; £4,500,000 underspend
findings.quote: A design partner for the facilities upgrade has been appointed. Works will commence after the lease agreement has been signed.

findings.headline: Theobalds Business Park Phase 2 development indefinitely on hold due to Google car park lease
findings.detail: Planning permission for a storage/distribution facility was granted in December 2023, but the development is now on hold because Google is leasing the site as a car park for its adjacent construction site. The £1m project is significantly underspent at £248k (£752k underspend), with no indication when it can resume.
findings.matters: An asset development project with planning permission is now indefinitely stalled by an external commercial agreement, creating uncertainty about capital deployment and whether the council's development strategy for this site can proceed.
findings.figures: £1,000,000 budget; £248,342 spent; £751,658 underspend
findings.quote: Although planning permission for construction of a storage or distribution facility was granted on 12 December 2023, the development of the site is currently on hold as Google is leasing the site as a car park for its adjacent construction site.

findings.headline: A departing planning officer caused six applications to miss statutory timescales in Q2
findings.detail: Of 121 planning applications determined in Q2, 17 went out of statutory time (14%). Six of these explicitly missed deadlines due to applications being reallocated following a planning team member leaving the council. This indicates turnover in a function critical to local development and capital projects.
findings.matters: Staffing losses and service disruptions in planning can delay key infrastructure and regeneration projects, affecting the council's capital programme execution and economic development plans.
findings.figures: 121 applications determined; 17 out of time (14%); 6 attributed to staff reallocation
findings.quote: The remaining six that went out of time were due to the cases being re-allocated to officers following a member of the team leaving the Council.

findings.headline: Formal complaints surged 79% with 49% upheld, heavily concentrated in council tax
findings.detail: Stage one formal complaints nearly doubled from 24 to 43, with 21 upheld. Council tax accounted for 12 of the 21 upheld complaints, with three planning, and two each for benefits and housing. This concentration suggests systemic issues in council tax billing or collections processes.
findings.matters: A 79% year-on-year increase in complaints with a 49% upheld rate indicates service delivery or governance failures; high volumes of upheld complaints in revenue-generating functions signal control weaknesses.
findings.figures: 43 complaints (up from 24, +79%), 21 upheld (49%), 12 council tax
findings.quote: There were 43 stage one formal complaints registered in quarter two 2025/26, compared to 24 in the same period of the previous year, 21 of which were upheld. In this quarter 12 of the upheld complaints were Council Tax, three were Planning, two upheld for both Benefits and Housing and one upheld for both Highways and Property.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation residents staying one month longer, signalling discharge difficulties and rising costs
findings.detail: Total households in temporary accommodation fell 8% to 184 from 199, but average length of stay increased by one month versus Q2 2024/25. Declining numbers paired with rising duration suggests cases are becoming more complex or permanent housing supply is constrained, driving higher per-case costs.
findings.matters: Extended temporary accommodation stays increase per-case costs in homelessness services; longer duration typically indicates difficulty accessing permanent housing or more complex support requirements.
findings.figures: 184 households (down 8% from 199); average length of stay increased by one month year-on-year
findings.quote: Those currently in TA have spent an average of one month more time residing than in quarter two of the previous year.

findings.headline: Business rates collection declined in Q2, below previous year and raising risk to the 97.8% annual target
findings.detail: Quarter two business rates collection reached 54.5%, down from 56.5% in Q2 2024/25. The annual target is 97.8%. While the council attributes this partly to timing of high-value properties added in August whose first payments were set for October 2025, the year-on-year decline still represents a revenue headwind.
findings.matters: Business rates are a significant council revenue source; quarterly decline raises the risk of missing the annual target and reducing available cash for services or debt service.
findings.figures: 54.5% (Q2 2025/26) vs 56.5% (Q2 2024/25); annual target 97.8%; 1.79% decrease reported
findings.quote: There was a slight improvement in council tax collection in quarter two (0.26%) and a 1.79% decrease in business rate collection. There were several high value properties added in August, whose first business rate payment were set for 1 October 2025.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation population growing, with asylum seeker residents nearly doubling year-on-year
findings.detail: 184 households in temporary accommodation at end of September 2025, up from 174 in September 2024. Of these, 49 were former asylum seekers compared to only 25 in the prior year — a 96% increase. The council is housing 275 individuals with complex support needs in TA, including 60 former asylum seekers registering with GPs, schools, applying for benefits.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is one of the most expensive services councils provide, typically £15,000-20,000+ per household annually. Rapid growth in asylum seeker residents signals increasing budget pressure from dispersal policy that lenders assess when evaluating financial resilience.
findings.figures: 184 households total (up from 174), 49 former asylum seekers (up from 25); 275 individuals with support needs recorded
findings.quote: At the end of September 2025, there were 184 households in TA this included 49 former asylum seekers. This compares to 174 households, of these 25 were former asylum seekers at the end of September 2024.

findings.headline: Investment income budget (£2.31m) nearly matches debt interest cost (£2.30m); yields expected to fall
findings.detail: 2026/27 budget has investment income and debt interest almost identical at £2.31m and £2.30m respectively. Council explicitly states investment yields will fall during 2026/27 interest rate cutting cycle, squeezing the narrow margin.
findings.matters: Council's net treasury income is near zero and vulnerable to compression; already expects this to occur during 2026/27
findings.figures: Investment income £2,310,000; debt interest £2,299,617; yields expected to fall in 2026/27
findings.quote: The budget for investment income in 2026/27 is £2,310,000 at an interest rate of 3.84%. The budget for debt interest paid in 2026/27 is £2,299,617... The Council has been advised that investment yields will fall during the interest rate cutting cycle in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Council funding capital programme from reserves rather than borrowing; investments declining
findings.detail: Council deliberately maintains under-borrowed position using cash reserves to fund capital. Long-term investments fell from £44m (March 2025) to £35m (December 2025)—a £9m reduction in 9 months. Document expects this decline to continue as capital programme progresses.
findings.matters: Shows the scale and sustainability of capital spending and the council's reliance on reserve depletion rather than borrowing—critical for assessing medium-term financial flexibility
findings.figures: £44m (31 March 2025) to £35m (31 December 2025); £51.65m capital financing requirement unfunded by borrowing
findings.quote: The Council is currently maintaining an under-borrowed position. This means that the capital borrowing need, (the Capital Financing Requirement), has not been fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Authority's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure. However, this will continue to reduce as the Council's agreed capital programme is delivered.

findings.headline: All £51.65m council debt matures April–September 2026 and must be refinanced
findings.detail: The entire debt portfolio consists of short-term loans from other local authorities with maturities concentrated in the next 6 months. The council's refinancing strategy assumes short-term borrowing remains cheaper than longer-dated debt.
findings.matters: Shows a material, near-term refinancing need that tests the council's market access and assumptions about rate conditions
findings.figures: £51.65 million, April to September 2026
findings.quote: The Council holds short term borrowing (its debt portfolio) of £51.65 million which has been principally financed by loans from other local authorities. These loans mature between April and September 2026 and will need to be refinanced.

findings.headline: Rental income protection reserve of £2.164m covers only 2-3 months of annual income
findings.detail: The council maintains a dedicated reserve to absorb short-term rental income shortfalls, but at £2.164m (as at 31 March 2025) it represents only 23-28% of a single year's projected rental income. Given that 28% of the budget depends on this income stream, the reserve provides limited cushion against sustained market stress or multiple tenant failures.
findings.matters: With budget dependency at 28%, a reserve covering only 2-3 months of that income may force service cuts or additional borrowing if property market conditions persist or tenant credit quality deteriorates
findings.figures: Rental income protection reserve £2.164m as at 31 March 2025; projected annual rental income £8.737m-£9.211m; reserve covers 2.3-2.8 months of income
findings.quote: In the unlikely event that rental income drops below the budgeted level the Council has a specific reserve in place (the rental income protection reserve), which could be used to address a short term shortfall in income. The balance of this reserve was £2.164 million as at 31 March 2025.

findings.headline: Commercial property income funds 28% of net service expenditure through the MTFS
findings.detail: The council's budget balance increasingly depends on commercial property rental income, which rises from 23% of net service expenditure in 2024/25 to 28% from 2025/26 onwards. The council explicitly states it uses this income as a substitute for service cuts, amid inflationary pressures and reduced government funding. Rental income is projected to dip to £8.737m in 2025/26 before recovering to £9.030m-£9.211m in 2026/27-2027/28.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that budget balance hinges on commercial property market performance; market downturn or major tenant failure could force unplanned service cuts or reserve depletion
findings.figures: 28% of net service expenditure (£8,737k-£9,211k rental income against £30,798k-£32,320k net service expenditure); 2024/25 actual rent £9,180k, 2025/26 projection £8,737k (4.8% decrease), 2026/27 estimate £9,030k
findings.quote: It chooses to do this in preference to reducing or cutting services, which would be necessary in order to set a balanced budget when expenditure is increasing due to inflationary pressures and changes in demand for services and government funding is reducing.

findings.paper_title: GENERAL FUND BUDGETS INCLUDING FEES AND CHARGES 202627_v2
findings.headline: Combined trading deficits at sports and leisure facilities increased from £477k to £555k, growing 16% year-on-year.
findings.detail: Broxbourne Sport and Spotlight leisure services are forecast to run combined deficits of £555k in 2026/27, up from £477k budgeted in 2025/26. Although membership numbers at sports sites are rising, the National Living Wage increase (4.1%) is offsetting revenue gains. These deficits are funded from business rates income.
findings.matters: Growing year-on-year subsidies of these services indicate pricing or operational constraints and represent an ongoing commitment of business rates revenue that reduces financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Broxbourne Sport £148k deficit, Spotlight £407k deficit, combined £555k versus £477k in 2025/26
findings.quote: The projected combined deficit for Broxbourne Sport (£148k) and the Spotlight (£407k) for 2026/27 is £555k; this is compared to a budgeted deficit in 2025/26 of £477k.

findings.paper_title: GENERAL FUND BUDGETS INCLUDING FEES AND CHARGES 202627_v2
findings.headline: BEST contract price increased by £1.2m to address past underfunding where price increases had not kept pace with inflation.
findings.detail: Broxbourne Environmental Services Trading (BEST) Ltd, the council's wholly owned subsidiary providing essential frontline services, had its contract price adjusted upward by £1.2m for 2026/27. A full contract review identified that previous price increases had not kept pace with inflation over time, creating financial imbalance within the subsidiary that had to be corrected.
findings.matters: This reveals that the council's contract management with its own critical service provider allowed significant funding gaps to accumulate, raising questions about financial oversight of service delivery sustainability.
findings.figures: £1.2m uplift in BEST contract price adjustment for 2026/27
findings.quote: previous contract price increases had not kept pace with inflation, resulting in a financial imbalance

findings.paper_title: GENERAL FUND BUDGETS INCLUDING FEES AND CHARGES 202627_v2
findings.headline: Council expects to be abolished in 2028 under proposed Local Government Reorganisation and has set aside £1m for transition costs.
findings.detail: The Government requires all Hertfordshire councils to prepare Local Government Reorganisation proposals. Broxbourne expects to be abolished in 2028 if Government proceeds with reorganisation following consultation in early 2026. The council has allocated up to £1m from its Service Protection and Enhancement Reserve (projected £3.8m balance) for reorganisation costs, though the final value and nature of the required contribution remain unquantified. The council must decide how to reset medium-term ambitions within the remaining lifespan of the organisation.
findings.matters: Structural uncertainty about the council's operational continuity within the medium term directly affects the security of long-term lending and the council's ability to manage existing obligations through potential transition.
findings.figures: Up to £1m allocated for LGR transition costs; Service Protection and Enhancement Reserve projected £3.8m; council abolition expected 2028
findings.quote: the current authority is expected to be abolished in 2028 if Government proceeds with reorganisation

news_drafts.headline: General Fund services overspent by £799k, only achieving balance through one-off grants and interest income
news_drafts.lead: The council's operational services ran approximately 9% over budget. The final surplus depends on interest income and discretionary grants, not on operational control. This suggests structural cost pressures or budget management challenges.

news_drafts.headline: £468k overspend in Property Services due to business rates on empty commercial properties and lost rental income
news_drafts.lead: Empty commercial property holdings represent dead weight on council finances and suggest either portfolio management issues or a struggling commercial real estate market in the borough. Lost rental income reduces the council's revenue base.

news_drafts.headline: Housing benefit subsidy shortfall of £642k due to temporary accommodation costs exceeding central government reimbursement
news_drafts.lead: This reveals structural demand pressure in temporary accommodation that the council cannot fully recoup. As homelessness continues to rise, this gap is likely to recur and widen.
